summary:
I built Ares Pathfinder, a web app for planning a safe walk outside on Mars. You pick a site: Gale crater, where Curiosity is driving; Jezero crater, where Perseverance is exploring; or two places further north, Deuteronilus Mensae and Arcadia Planitia, that only orbiters have seen so far. Ares Pathfinder shows you the real ground in 3D, colours it green, yellow or red by how safe it is to walk on, and finds the safest way to a science stop and back before your oxygen or daylight runs out.

Then you can actually do it. Ride a crewed rover part of the way while its screen shows whether the ground under the wheels is safe, then walk the last stretch in a NASA suit, seen from behind, from the side or through the helmet. Ingenuity can fly just ahead of you along the route, or scout any spot and come back to land where it took off, staying within the limits of its 72 real flights. Live NASA feeds show where the rovers are right now, their latest photos, the weather and any solar storms on the way.

Everything is built on real mission data from NASA, ESA and the UAE's Hope mission, and anything I had to estimate is clearly marked. I think the first people on Mars will need exactly this: one clear picture of ground nobody has walked on yet.
details:
I wanted to answer a simple question an astronaut on Mars will ask every morning: can I walk over there and get back safely today, and which way should I go?

Ares Pathfinder works at four real places. At Gale and Jezero craters, Curiosity and Perseverance have already driven over the ground, so I can check my maps against what the rovers actually found. Deuteronilus Mensae and Arcadia Planitia are possible future landing areas that only orbiters have seen, so everything there is shown as a prediction.

When you open a site you see the real terrain in 3D, built from HiRISE, CTX and HRSC images and height maps. Every 10 to 20 metres of ground is coloured green (safe), yellow (take care) or red (no-go), based on slope, roughness, terrain type and real boulders I mapped from HiRISE pictures. Pick a science stop, like Cheyava Falls at Jezero, and Ares Pathfinder finds the safest route there and back. It checks the route against oxygen, daylight, temperature, radiation dose and the weight of the suit and kit. If a place can't be reached on foot, it tells you. Right now, for example, Perseverance is outside Jezero's rim, and the rim is too steep for someone in a suit to walk down.

After planning you can do the walk. A crewed rover can drive the first part while its screen shows whether the ground under the wheels is green, yellow or red. Then an astronaut in a NASA suit walks the rest over the real ground while oxygen, distance and time to sunset tick along. You can watch from behind, from the side or through the helmet, which only shows what matters for safety: air left, sunset, dust, sun storms, radiation, the path and the next stop. Ingenuity can fly just ahead of you along the route, or scout any spot, even one that is unsafe on foot, and fly back to land where it took off. I kept its height, speed and range within what it managed in its 72 real flights, and you can replay any of those flights on their recorded paths. Live feeds show where the rovers are today, their newest raw photos, Mars weather from REMS and MEDA, solar storm alerts from DONKI and which Deep Space Network dishes are talking to Mars.

Why it matters: all this information exists today, but it's spread across dozens of missions, file formats and websites. I pulled it into one picture you can read in a few seconds, whether it's on a habitat wall screen, a tablet or a helmet display. I hope it's useful to mission planners and students as well as future crews.

How I built it: the app is TypeScript with Next.js and React. MapLibre GL draws the 3D terrain, three.js draws the suit and the helicopter, and route finding runs in a Web Worker using an A* search over a cost grid. Behind it is a Python pipeline (GDAL, rasterio, NumPy) that downloads the mission data, lines it up and cuts it into map tiles. There are 384 automated tests, and I checked every screen in the browser.

What I was careful about: I only used real data, so there are no made-up rocks, places or readings, and every layer says where it came from. A few things have to be estimated, and the app says so wherever they appear. Oxygen use, effort and heart rate come from a model based on NASA suit and Apollo data. Radiation dose uses the average that Curiosity's RAD instrument measured. Future conditions are based on past seasons at the same time of year. My 6° and 15° slope limits are planning values based on NASA suited-walking tests, not an official NASA rule. I also kept the wording plain, so a tired astronaut can read a screen at a glance, with the technical details one tap away.

HiRISE images and terrain models (MRO, University of Arizona)
Jezero HiRISE 1 m height map (Mars 2020 team, USGS)
USGS geologic map of Jezero crater (SIM 3464)
Curiosity rover waypoints and drive path (MMGIS)
Perseverance rover waypoints and drive path (MMGIS)
THEMIS thermal inertia mosaic (Mars Odyssey, USGS)
NASA 3D Resources (Mark III suit, Ingenuity, MRO, Mars Odyssey models)
Curiosity's Proposed Path up Mount Sharp
projectRefs: ESA Mars Express HRSC height maps (ESA/DLR/FU Berlin, via PDS)
ESA ExoMars TGO CaSSIS colour images (ESA Planetary Science Archive)
ESA Mars Express OMEGA and MRO CRISM water-made minerals (Carter et al. 2013, via Mars Trek)
UAE Emirates Mars Mission (Hope) EMIRS and EXI data
LMD Mars dust climatology (Montabone et al.)
MBARS boulder measurement method (Hood et al. 2022)
THEMIS thermal inertia (Edwards and Buz, Zenodo)
TES and IRTM rock abundance map service (Arizona State University)
IAU / USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (place names)
Claude Code by Anthropic (AI coding assistant used during development)
CMU Graphics Lab Motion Capture Database (human walk)
